title: Run the application on a VPS
summary: Manage the Java process with a dedicated user, configuration and systemd.

sources.title: Engineering Digest: How to Host Spring Boot on VPS: Production Guide (2026)

richText: Prepare the application host
A virtual private server (VPS) provides a machine that you manage.
Install a Java runtime compatible with the application’s Boot release and compiled classes.
Build the JAR from a known application revision and copy that artifact to the server.
Use a dedicated operating-system user with access to the application’s required files.
Supply database settings and other credentials through restricted configuration.
Let systemd manage the process
systemd is a Linux service manager.
A service unit describes the command to run and how to start or restart it.
It can start the application during boot and restart it after failure.
Starting Java in an interactive terminal does not provide these service settings.

example.title: Create a service for the journal JAR
description: The server has systemd and Java installed at /usr/bin/java.
Create the journal user, /opt/journal directory and /etc/journal.env before starting this unit.
Copy journal.jar into /opt/journal and let the journal user read it.
For the next reverse-proxy lesson, put SERVER_ADDRESS=127.0.0.1 and SERVER_PORT=8080 in /etc/journal.env.
Add required database settings to that file and restrict access because it can contain credentials.
example.code:
# /etc/systemd/system/journal.service
[Unit]
Description=Journal application
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
User=journal
WorkingDirectory=/opt/journal
EnvironmentFile=/etc/journal.env
ExecStart=/usr/bin/java -jar /opt/journal/journal.jar
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
explanation: User selects the operating-system account that runs Java.
EnvironmentFile supplies environment variables to the process.
Restart=on-failure restarts a failed process after five seconds.
daemon-reload makes systemd reread the unit. enable --now starts it and enables boot-time startup.
status and journalctl show whether the process started and what it logged.
example.commands:
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now journal.service
systemctl status journal.service
journalctl -u journal.service

richText: Diagnose startup failures
If the process repeatedly restarts, read its logs before changing the restart settings.
Check the Java version, required settings and database availability.
Keep application logs available and configure their retention.
After a controlled restart or reboot, confirm the service starts again.
Update the deployed artifact
Keep the current artifact available before replacing it.
Restart the service after installing a new JAR. Check startup and an application request.
Plan database migrations and backups separately from JAR replacement.
